newsitem.title: GERMANY: German politicians want to block non-EU workers.
newsitem.headline: German politicians want to block non-EU workers.

text.p: Members of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's ruling Christian Democrats (CDU) want to make it harder for non-European Union foreigners to work in Germany to help tackle record unemployment, two magazines reported on Monday.

Spiegel and Focus weekly news magazines said a labour and welfare parliamentary working group of the CDU and Bavarian sister party the Christian Social Union (CSU) outlined the demand in a paper which had not yet been published.
The magazines said the group want to make it harder for foreigners, including visiting students, seasonal labourers and relations of those already in Germany, to get work permits.

It also wants to minimise the number of asylum seekers coming to Germany, particularly those who had passed through a third "safe" country. "It is necessary to counter an overburdening of the labour market through a continued influx from third countries," Spiegel quoted the paper as saying.
But head of the working group, the CDU's Julius Louven, told Reuters the group was still working on the paper and said it would only be presented to party leaders after Easter.
Louven dismissed as pure speculation proposals listed in the magazines including limiting the number of Jewish immigrants from the former Soviet Union to the country.
But leader of Germany's Jewish community Ignatz Bubis reacted angrily to the proposals, calling them populist.

In a release ahead of publication of Tuesday's edition, Berlin's Tageszeitung quoted Bubis as saying lengthy application procedures were an indirect quota system for regulating the number of former Soviet Jews coming to Germany.

Around 60,000 Jews have come to Germany since Chancellor Kohl agreed in 1990 to accept an unlimited number from the former Soviet Union for humanitarian reasons, but Bubis said some 130,000 applications were still waiting for approval.
Last year the government denied reports it was considering changing this policy because most of the immigrants were no longer persecuted and sought to emigrate for economic reasons.

The opposition Greens called the proposals "tasteless and unashamed". "Union politicians are making Jews the scapegoats for the desolate labour market situation. That is breaking a political taboo," said Volker Beck, Greens justice spokesman.

The conservative CSU has already proposed restrictions on work permits and in January CSU leader Finance Minister Theo Waigel said it was "grotesque" that so many foreigners were working in Germany, while so many Germans were out of work.
German unemployment hit a post-war record of 4.7 million in February.

Focus said other proposals by the group included speeding up the repatriation of thousands of Bosnian refugees, demanding that aspiring settlers with German origins be able to speak German and restricting the number of foreign seasonal workers a firm would be allowed to employ.
Germany started the forcible repatriation last October of over 300,000 Bosnian refugees who it had hoped would leave of their own accord.
